subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity
intro: Read each passage closely before answering. These questions ask you to connect several details, not to copy one sentence. You may need to infer a character's feeling, motive, or trait, trace a cause-and-effect link, figure out a word's meaning from context, or sum up the gist of the whole passage. Use only what the text supports.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The whole class had voted to keep the class hamster in Room 12, and Dev had been the loudest voice for it. So when the cage door swung open one morning and the hamster was gone, everyone looked at Dev. He had been the last one to feed it the night before. For the rest of the day he checked behind every shelf and bookcase, refusing to go to recess, whispering the hamster's name into the dark gaps along the wall. He did not eat his lunch. When the janitor finally found the hamster curled behind a heater, Dev's shoulders dropped, and he laughed for the first time all day."

What can you most reasonably infer about why Dev searched so hard for the hamster all day? Explain using two details from the passage.
items.answer: Dev felt responsible for the hamster's escape and guilty about it, so he searched all day to make things right. He had argued loudest to keep the hamster and was the last one to feed it the night before, so he likely felt the loss was his fault.

steps: The passage never states Dev's feeling directly, so this is an inference that must be built from his actions and the facts around him.
Two facts point to responsibility: Dev 'had been the loudest voice' for keeping the hamster, and he 'had been the last one to feed it the night before,' which is when the cage was likely left open.
His behavior, skipping recess and lunch and searching every shelf, shows the loss matters to him personally, not just casually.
His shoulders dropping and his first laugh when the hamster is found confirm the worry lifting, supporting that guilt and responsibility drove the search.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"For weeks the drought had baked the garden hard as brick. The bean plants Lena had started from seed leaned over, their leaves curled and gray. Each evening she carried water from the rain barrel, one careful cup at a time, even though the barrel was nearly empty. Her brother told her the plants were finished and she should stop wasting water. Lena said nothing and kept watering. On the ninth morning, when the first real rain in a month drummed on the roof, she ran outside in her socks to see the beans drinking it in, their leaves already lifting toward the sky."

Based on the whole passage, what does it most reveal about Lena's character? Support your answer with details.
items.answer: Lena is determined and hopeful; she does not give up even when success looks unlikely. She kept carrying water one cup at a time though the barrel was nearly empty and her brother said the plants were finished, and her joy at the rain shows her hope was rewarded.

steps: The question asks for a character trait, which is an inference drawn from how Lena acts across the passage.
She keeps watering 'one careful cup at a time' even though the barrel is 'nearly empty' and her brother says the plants are 'finished,' which shows persistence against discouragement.
She says nothing and keeps watering rather than arguing, showing quiet determination rather than stubbornness for its own sake.
Running outside in her socks to watch the beans revive shows her hope, and the leaves 'lifting toward the sky' rewards it. Together these details reveal a determined, hopeful character.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Theo had borrowed his sister's bike without asking, just to ride to the corner store. On the way back, the front tire hit a pothole and the rim bent so the wheel scraped with every turn. He could have left the bike in the garage and said nothing; she rarely rode it. Instead he wheeled it straight to her room, told her exactly what had happened, and offered to pay for the repair from his savings. She was angry for a moment, then surprised, then almost smiling."

What caused Theo's sister to go from angry to almost smiling? Explain the cause-and-effect link.
items.answer: Theo's honesty caused his sister's reaction to soften. Because he could have hidden the damage but instead told her the truth right away and offered to pay for the repair, her anger gave way to surprise and an almost-smile.

steps: The question targets cause and effect: what made the sister's feeling change.
The effect is the shift 'angry for a moment, then surprised, then almost smiling.'
The cause is in the prior sentences: Theo 'could have left the bike in the garage and said nothing,' but instead he told her 'exactly what had happened' and offered to pay.
His unexpected honesty and willingness to make it right are what surprise her and soften the anger, so the cause is his choice to own the mistake.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The path up the headland was little more than a goat track, slick with spray. As the cliff steepened, the children could no longer walk upright; they had to clamber, gripping tufts of grass and jamming their sneakers into cracks in the rock, pulling themselves up hand over hand. Below them the sea boiled white against the stones, and no one looked down twice."

What does the word "clamber" mean as it is used in this passage? Explain how the context tells you.
items.answer: "Clamber" means to climb awkwardly and with effort, using both hands and feet. The passage says they could no longer walk upright and had to grip grass, jam their sneakers into cracks, and pull themselves up hand over hand, which describes effortful climbing.

steps: The question asks for word meaning from context, so we look at the surrounding description rather than the sound of the word.
Just before 'clamber,' the text says 'the children could no longer walk upright,' signaling a movement different from walking.
The details that follow define it: 'gripping tufts of grass,' 'jamming their sneakers into cracks,' and 'pulling themselves up hand over hand.'
All of this describes climbing a steep slope with hands and feet and effort, so 'clamber' means to climb awkwardly using hands and feet.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Every winter the lighthouse keeper, Old Bram, climbed two hundred steps to trim the lamp, though the town had long since switched the harbor to electric beacons. Ships did not need his light anymore. Still, each dusk it bloomed gold across the water. The new families in town called him foolish. But the fishermen who had grown up in those waters left bread and salt on his step, and on the foggiest nights they steered a little closer to the old gold glow, the one they had trusted since they were boys."

Which statement best summarizes the central idea of this passage, and why?
items.answer: The passage's central idea is that Old Bram's lighthouse, though no longer needed, still has real value to the people who grew up trusting it. Newcomers call him foolish, but the local fishermen honor him and still steer toward his light, showing that something old can still matter.

steps: The task is to summarize the central idea of the whole passage, not restate one detail.
A key tension runs through it: the light is technically unnecessary ('Ships did not need his light anymore') yet Bram keeps it burning.
The newcomers 'called him foolish,' but the fishermen who grew up there leave bread and salt and 'steered a little closer' on foggy nights.
Pulling these together, the gist is that the old light still holds value and trust for those who know it, so the central idea is about the lasting worth of something seemingly outdated.

items.prompt:
Read this poem.

"The kite tugs hard against the string,
impatient as a colt to run,
yet every time it climbs too high
the wind forgets it, one by one.
It dives, it sulks along the grass,
then lifts again with stubborn pride,
as if the only way to fly
is first to fall, and then decide."

What does the poem suggest about flying, or about trying in general? Explain using the poem's words.
items.answer: The poem suggests that succeeding, or flying, often means failing first and then choosing to try again. The kite 'dives' and 'sulks,' then 'lifts again with stubborn pride,' and the closing lines say the only way to fly is 'first to fall, and then decide.'

steps: This is a poem, so we read for the idea built through its images rather than a single literal statement.
The kite is described like a living thing: 'impatient as a colt,' and it 'sulks' when it falls, which casts flying as a struggle with setbacks.
The pattern is fall, then rise: it 'dives' and then 'lifts again with stubborn pride.'
The last two lines state the theme: 'the only way to fly / is first to fall, and then decide,' meaning persistence after failure is what leads to success.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Mr. Alvarez handed back the math quizzes face down, the way he always did. Around her, Jada heard the small sounds of paper flipping and a few groans. She did not turn hers over. She slid it into her folder, zipped the folder shut, and stared straight ahead at the whiteboard, where yesterday's homework still glowed in faded marker. When the boy beside her asked what she got, she just shrugged and said the eraser on her pencil had worn down to nothing."

What can you most reasonably infer about how Jada feels about her quiz score? Explain how you know.
items.answer: Jada most likely feels upset or ashamed about her score and does not want anyone to know it. She refuses to even look at the quiz, zips it away unseen, and dodges her classmate's question by changing the subject to her pencil eraser.

steps: The feeling is never stated, so this is an inference from Jada's behavior.
She does not turn the quiz over while others do, and she 'slid it into her folder, zipped the folder shut,' which shows she does not want to see or share the result.
When asked her score, she 'just shrugged' and gave an unrelated answer about her eraser, which is a way to avoid the question.
Avoiding the score and deflecting the question together suggest disappointment or shame about how she did.

items.prompt:
Read this short scene.

CORA: You left the campsite map at home, didn't you.
MILO: I have it up here. (taps his head) I've walked this trail a hundred times.
CORA: That was in summer. Half these markers are buried.
MILO: (pausing at a fork, looking left, then right) ... The river should be on our left.
CORA: Milo. We crossed the river an hour ago.
MILO: (quietly) Right. Of course. The river. (He turns and starts back the way they came.)

What can the reader infer about Milo by the end of the scene? Support your answer with lines from the scene.
items.answer: By the end, the reader can infer that Milo is lost and finally admitting it, even though he started out overconfident. He boasted he had the map 'up here' and had walked the trail 'a hundred times,' but he pauses confused at the fork, gets the river wrong, and quietly turns back the way they came.

steps: In drama we infer character from dialogue and stage directions.
Milo begins confident, claiming the map is 'up here' and that he has walked the trail 'a hundred times,' so at first he seems sure.
The stage direction shows doubt: he is 'pausing at a fork, looking left, then right,' and he misremembers where the river is.
His quiet 'Right. Of course' and turning 'back the way they came' show he now realizes he is lost, revealing that his confidence was misplaced.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"Nadia had planned the surprise party for a month: the streamers, the cake, the friends crammed silently in the dark living room. But her brother's flight was delayed, and delayed again, until the candles had burned to stubs and half the guests had drifted home. When he finally walked in at midnight, only Nadia was left, sitting on the floor beside a sagging cake. He looked at the streamers, then at her, and instead of the loud welcome she had imagined, the house was quiet. 'You waited,' he said softly, and that, somehow, was better than any crowd."

Why does the ending feel meaningful even though the party fell apart? Explain the cause-and-effect connection.
items.answer: The ending feels meaningful because the failed plan led to something more personal. Because the flight delays emptied the house, only Nadia was left, and her brother's quiet 'You waited' showed he valued her loyalty more than the crowd, which 'was better than any crowd.'

steps: The question asks how a cause (the party falling apart) leads to a meaningful effect.
The delays are the cause of the change: candles 'burned to stubs' and 'half the guests had drifted home,' so the big party did not happen.
The effect is that 'only Nadia was left,' turning a crowd event into a one-on-one moment.
Her brother's reaction, 'You waited,' shows he is moved by her loyalty, and the text says this 'was better than any crowd,' so the collapse of the plan caused a more meaningful ending.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The new student, Ravi, ate lunch alone for the first week, a book always open beside his tray. On Thursday a soccer ball rolled to his feet in the courtyard. He stopped it, looked at the group of players, and for a moment seemed about to kick it back and walk over. Then he just nudged it gently in their direction and returned to his book. By the next Monday, though, he was sitting at the edge of their table, still quiet, but laughing once at something someone said."

How does Ravi change over the course of the passage? Use details to explain.
items.answer: Ravi slowly moves from keeping to himself toward joining the group. At first he eats alone with a book and only nudges the ball back without approaching, but by the next Monday he sits at the edge of the players' table and laughs once at a joke, showing he is starting to connect.

steps: The question asks about change over time, so we compare Ravi at the start and at the end.
At the start he is isolated: he 'ate lunch alone' with 'a book always open,' and when the ball comes he only 'nudged it gently' and went back to reading instead of joining.
By the next Monday he is 'sitting at the edge of their table' and 'laughing once,' which is closer than before.
The shift from sitting alone to sitting near the group and sharing a laugh shows he is gradually opening up, even though he is 'still quiet.'

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The audition list was taped to the gym door, and a knot of dancers pressed close to read it. Salome did not push forward. She waited until the hallway emptied, then walked up alone and ran her finger down the names. Hers was near the bottom, in the chorus, not the solo she had trained six months for. She read it twice. Then she squared her shoulders, took a slow breath, and said, half to herself, 'Chorus this year. Solo next year.' She picked up her bag and walked to practice without looking back."

What character trait does Salome show in this passage? Explain using her words and actions.
items.answer: Salome shows resilience and a positive, forward-looking attitude. Although she did not get the solo she trained six months for, she squares her shoulders, tells herself 'Chorus this year. Solo next year,' and heads to practice 'without looking back' instead of giving up.

steps: The question asks for a trait, inferred from how Salome responds to disappointment.
The setback is clear: her name is 'in the chorus, not the solo she had trained six months for,' so she has reason to be discouraged.
Her actions show composure: she 'squared her shoulders,' took 'a slow breath,' and walked on 'without looking back.'
Her words 'Chorus this year. Solo next year' reframe the loss as a step toward a future goal, which together with her actions reveals resilience.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"The old fishing village clung to its stories the way the boats clung to their moorings in a storm. No matter how the tide of new ideas pulled at the town, the elders held fast, repeating the same legends each festival night until even the youngest children could finish the endings. Some called it stubbornness. The harbormaster called it an anchor, the thing that kept the village from drifting into the wide gray sea of forgetting."

What does the harbormaster mean by calling the village's old stories "an anchor"? Explain the figurative language.
items.answer: The harbormaster means the old stories keep the village steady and connected to its identity, the way an anchor keeps a boat from drifting. He says they keep the village 'from drifting into the wide gray sea of forgetting,' so the stories hold the community in place against losing its past.

steps: This question asks about figurative meaning, so we should not read 'anchor' literally as a metal hook.
The passage builds a sea comparison: the village 'clung to its stories the way the boats clung to their moorings,' and new ideas are a 'tide' that pulls at the town.
An anchor's real job is to hold a boat steady, so calling the stories an anchor means they hold the village steady.
The phrase 'kept the village from drifting into the wide gray sea of forgetting' tells us the anchor protects the town's memory and identity, which is what the figurative language means.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"At first the science fair seemed like a punishment to Owen. He grumbled when his teacher assigned it, and he chose the easiest topic he could find. But when his model volcano fizzled instead of erupting, he stayed after school to figure out why. He read about chemical reactions. He rebuilt it twice. By the night of the fair, Owen was the one explaining his project to a crowd, talking faster than anyone, pointing at his charts with a grin. 'I might do chemistry next year,' he told his mom on the way home, surprising them both."

Which statement best summarizes the central idea of this passage, and why?
items.answer: The central idea is that Owen's reluctant project turned into a genuine interest once he worked through its problems. He started out grumbling and picked the easiest topic, but after his volcano failed he kept rebuilding it and learning, and by the end he was excited and considering chemistry next year.

steps: The task is to capture the gist of the whole passage, tracing Owen's arc rather than one moment.
At the start the fair 'seemed like a punishment'; he 'grumbled' and chose 'the easiest topic he could find.'
The turning point is the failed volcano, after which he 'stayed after school,' read about reactions, and 'rebuilt it twice,' showing growing investment.
By the end he is eagerly explaining his work and says 'I might do chemistry next year,' so the central idea is that effort transformed a chore into real interest.

items.prompt:
Read the passage.

"For years the meadow behind the school had been a tangle of weeds and litter. Then Ms. Okafor's class began the restoration: pulling invasive vines, planting milkweed, hauling buckets of water through the dry weeks of August. The work was slow and few people noticed. But one September morning, a single monarch butterfly drifted over the new milkweed, then another, then a dozen, their wings flickering orange against the green. The students stood very still, hardly breathing, as if a loud sound might undo the whole fragile miracle they had made."

What does the word "restoration" mean as it is used in this passage? Use context to explain.
items.answer: "Restoration" means the work of bringing the meadow back to a healthy, natural state. The context shows the students pulling invasive vines, planting milkweed, and watering through August so that butterflies returned, which is the act of repairing and renewing the damaged meadow.

steps: We determine the meaning from the surrounding description, not from guessing at the word's parts.
Before 'restoration' the meadow is described as 'a tangle of weeds and litter,' so something is being fixed.
The word is immediately followed by the actions it names: 'pulling invasive vines, planting milkweed, hauling buckets of water.'
These actions repair and revive the land, and the return of monarchs shows the result, so 'restoration' means the act of bringing the meadow back to a healthy state.

items.prompt:
Read this short scene.

MAYA: You're really not coming to the recital?
DAD: (not looking up from his laptop) I have that deadline, Maya. You know how it is.
MAYA: It's the violin solo. The one I told you about in March.
DAD: I'll catch the next one. Send me a video.
MAYA: (after a silence) There isn't a next one. It's the last concert of the year. (She picks up her case and goes to the door.) Don't worry about the video. (The door clicks shut. DAD finally looks up at the empty doorway.)

What does the final stage direction suggest about the father, and how do you know?
items.answer: The final stage direction suggests the father suddenly realizes he made a mistake by brushing off Maya. He keeps his eyes on his laptop the whole time, but only after she leaves and says there is no next concert does he 'finally look up at the empty doorway,' showing the moment of regret has come too late.

steps: In drama, stage directions carry meaning we must interpret.
Throughout the scene the father is 'not looking up from his laptop,' showing he is not really paying attention to Maya.
The contrast comes at the end: he 'finally looks up,' but only 'at the empty doorway,' after she has already gone.
Because he looks up only once it is too late and the door has clicked shut, the direction suggests he now realizes the cost of ignoring her, a regret that arrives a moment too late.
